questions.question: In 1829, Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner noticed that when three elements with similar properties are written in order of increasing atomic mass, the atomic mass of the middle element is roughly the ______ of the masses of the other two elements. A student in Asmara then writes the triad Lithium ($$6.9\text{ u}$$), Sodium ($$23.0\text{ u}$$), Potassium ($$39.0\text{ u}$$) and reports that the expected mass of the middle element is $$45.9\text{ u}$$. (a) Fill in the blank in Döbereiner's rule. (b) Calculate the correct expected mass of the middle element and point out the student's mistake.

solution_steps.title: Recall the definition of a Döbereiner triad
solution_steps.detail: Döbereiner grouped elements in threes (triads) so that the three members had similar properties, and he observed that the atomic mass of the middle element was approximately the average (arithmetic mean) of the atomic masses of the outer two elements. So the missing word in the statement is 'average' (arithmetic mean).

solution_steps.title: Write the triad rule as a formula
solution_steps.detail: For the triad Li, Na, K, the rule gives: Mass of Na $$\approx \dfrac{\text{Mass of Li} + \text{Mass of K}}{2}$$.

solution_steps.title: Substitute the given masses
solution_steps.detail: Substitute Li $$= 6.9\text{ u}$$ and K $$= 39.0\text{ u}$$ into the formula: Mass of Na $$\approx \dfrac{6.9 + 39.0}{2}$$.

solution_steps.title: Carry out the division correctly
solution_steps.detail: Add the outer masses: $$6.9 + 39.0 = 45.9\text{ u}$$. The rule then requires dividing this sum by 2: $$\dfrac{45.9}{2} = 22.95\text{ u}$$, which rounds to $$23.0\text{ u}$$.

solution_steps.title: Identify the student's error
solution_steps.detail: The student's value of $$45.9\text{ u}$$ is simply the sum of the two outer masses; the student forgot to divide by 2, which is the step that produces the average. The correct expected mass is therefore $$22.95\text{ u} \approx 23.0\text{ u}$$.

solution_steps.title: State the conclusion
solution_steps.detail: The blank is 'average (arithmetic mean)'. The correct expected mass of the middle element is about $$23.0\text{ u}$$, exactly the actual atomic mass of Sodium, so the Li-Na-K triad satisfies Döbereiner's rule; the student should have divided the sum by 2.

questions.answer: (a) average (arithmetic mean). (b) Expected mass $$= \dfrac{6.9 + 39.0}{2} = 22.95\text{ u} \approx 23.0\text{ u}$$, which matches Sodium. The student's mistake was to report the sum $$45.9\text{ u}$$ without dividing by 2.

similar_questions.question: Sulfur ($$S = 32.1\text{ u}$$), Selenium ($$Se = 79.0\text{ u}$$) and Tellurium ($$Te = 127.6\text{ u}$$) are members of the same chemical family. Use Döbereiner's triad rule to work out the mass that the middle element 'should' have, compare it with Selenium's actual mass of $$79.0\text{ u}$$, and state one reason why Döbereiner's triad system was eventually abandoned.
similar_questions.answer: The rule gives $$\dfrac{32.1 + 127.6}{2} = 79.85\text{ u} \approx 79.9\text{ u}$$, which is close to Selenium's actual mass of $$79.0\text{ u}$$, so the triad rule holds approximately. The system was abandoned because it could be applied to only a few elements, not to all known elements.

solution_steps.title: Identify the middle element
solution_steps.detail: The three elements in order of increasing mass are S ($$32.1\text{ u}$$), Se ($$79.0\text{ u}$$), and Te ($$127.6\text{ u}$$), so Selenium is the middle member and its mass should be about the mean of the other two.

solution_steps.title: Apply the triad formula
solution_steps.detail: Mass of Se $$\approx \dfrac{\text{mass of S} + \text{mass of Te}}{2} = \dfrac{32.1 + 127.6}{2}$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare with the actual mass
solution_steps.detail: The predicted $$79.9\text{ u}$$ differs from the actual $$79.0\text{ u}$$ by only about $$0.9\text{ u}$$, which is a close agreement, so the triad rule works reasonably well for this family.

solution_steps.title: State the limitation of the triad system
solution_steps.detail: Despite such successes, Döbereiner could not fit all elements into triads; the system applied only to a few elements and was therefore of limited use, which pushed chemists to look for a broader classification such as Mendeleev's table.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes to the S-Se-Te family, supplies Selenium's actual mass so the task becomes a comparison of prediction with experiment, and adds the limitation of the triad system; the main question instead asks for a definition and error-spotting in the Li-Na-K triad.

similar_questions.question: Döbereiner's rule can also be rearranged. If Lithium ($$6.9\text{ u}$$) and Sodium ($$23.0\text{ u}$$) are the first and middle members of a triad, use the mean relationship to predict the atomic mass of the third (heavier) member, and name that element.
similar_questions.answer: Mass of the third member $$= 2(23.0) - 6.9 = 39.1\text{ u}$$, which identifies the element as Potassium ($$K$$).

solution_steps.title: Write the mean relationship
solution_steps.detail: The triad rule states: Mass of Na $$= \dfrac{\text{Mass of Li} + \text{Mass of X}}{2}$$, where X is the unknown heavier member.

solution_steps.title: Rearrange for the unknown
solution_steps.detail: Multiply both sides by 2: $$2 \times \text{Mass of Na} = \text{Mass of Li} + \text{Mass of X}$$. Then subtract the mass of Li: Mass of X $$= 2 \times \text{Mass of Na} - \text{Mass of Li}$$.

solution_steps.title: Identify the element and conclude
solution_steps.detail: An atomic mass of $$39.1\text{ u}$$ corresponds to Potassium ($$39.0\text{ u}$$ given in the triad), so X is Potassium. This confirms the Li-Na-K triad from the other direction.

similar_questions.variant_note: Keeps the Li-Na-K triad but reverses the algebra: instead of averaging the outer two masses, the mean equation is rearranged to find the heavy member from the first and middle members.

questions.question: The chemistry club at Asmara's Semaetat Secondary School built a wall chart of the M shell (the third principal energy level). How many subshells does the M shell contain, and what is its total electron capacity according to the $$2n^2$$ rule?

solution_steps.title: Recall the rule linking subshells to the shell number
solution_steps.detail: The chapter states that the number of subshells in a shell is equal to its principal quantum number $$n$$. For the third shell (M shell), $$n = 3$$, so there must be 3 subshells.

solution_steps.title: Name the subshells of the third shell
solution_steps.detail: Subshells are labelled $$s, p, d, f$$ in order. For $$n = 3$$ they are $$3s$$, $$3p$$ and $$3d$$. An $$f$$ subshell first appears in the fourth shell ($$4f$$), so option C is wrong.

solution_steps.title: Add the subshell capacities
solution_steps.detail: The maximum capacities are 2 electrons for $$s$$, 6 for $$p$$ and 10 for $$d$$. Therefore: $$2 + 6 + 10 = 18$$ electrons in the M shell.

solution_steps.title: Check with the $$2n^2$$ formula
solution_steps.detail: Total shell capacity $$= 2n^2 = 2 \times 3^2 = 2 \times 9 = 18$$ electrons, which agrees with the subshell sum. Option E fails because it wrongly gives 32.

solution_steps.title: Select the correct option
solution_steps.detail: The M shell has 3 subshells ($$3s, 3p, 3d$$) and a total capacity of 18 electrons, which is option B.

similar_questions.question: How many subshells are present in the N shell ($$n = 4$$) of an atom, what are their designations, and what is the total electron capacity of this shell?
similar_questions.answer: 4 subshells ($$4s, 4p, 4d, 4f$$) with a total capacity of 32 electrons.

solution_steps.title: Use the subshell-count rule
solution_steps.detail: Number of subshells $$= n$$; here $$n = 4$$, so the N shell contains 4 subshells.

solution_steps.title: List the designations
solution_steps.detail: Following the $$s, p, d, f$$ sequence for $$n = 4$$ gives $$4s, 4p, 4d$$ and $$4f$$.

solution_steps.title: Sum the subshell capacities
solution_steps.detail: Capacities are 2, 6, 10 and 14 electrons respectively: $$2 + 6 + 10 + 14 = 32$$ electrons.

solution_steps.title: Confirm with $$2n^2$$
solution_steps.detail: $$2n^2 = 2 \times 4^2 = 2 \times 16 = 32$$ electrons, so the answer is confirmed.

similar_questions.variant_note: Shifted from the M shell ($$n = 3$$) to the N shell ($$n = 4$$), so the number of subshells and the capacity both change.

similar_questions.question: An $$s$$ subshell and a $$p$$ subshell are completely filled with electrons. State the maximum number of electrons each can hold, and calculate the total number of electrons held by the two filled subshells together.
similar_questions.answer: A filled $$s$$ subshell holds 2 electrons and a filled $$p$$ subshell holds 6 electrons, giving a total of 8 electrons.

solution_steps.title: State the capacity of an $$s$$ subshell
solution_steps.detail: From the chapter's capacity table, an $$s$$ subshell can hold a maximum of 2 electrons.

solution_steps.title: State the capacity of a $$p$$ subshell
solution_steps.detail: A $$p$$ subshell can hold a maximum of 6 electrons.

solution_steps.title: Add the two capacities
solution_steps.detail: Total $$= 2 + 6 = 8$$ electrons. This is exactly the capacity of the L shell ($$n = 2$$, $$2s$$ and $$2p$$).

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the task from a whole-shell count to individual subshell capacities, using the same capacity facts in a simpler, more direct form.

questions.question: A sample of an Eritrean mineral contains an element whose complete electron configuration is $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2 3d^1$$. (a) Identify the element and state its atomic number. (b) Write its abbreviated (noble gas) electron configuration. (c) State, with justification, whether it is a representative element, a transition element or an inner transition element.

solution_steps.title: Count the total number of electrons
solution_steps.detail: Add the superscripts in the configuration: $$2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 1 = 21$$ electrons. A neutral atom has electrons equal to its protons, so the atomic number $$Z = 21$$.

solution_steps.title: Identify the element
solution_steps.detail: The element with atomic number 21 is Scandium ($$Sc$$), so the mineral contains Scandium.

solution_steps.title: Choose the correct noble-gas core
solution_steps.detail: The noble gas in the row directly above Scandium is Argon ($$Z = 18$$), whose configuration is $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6$$. This matches the first six terms of the full configuration exactly, so it can be replaced by $$[\text{Ar}]$$.

solution_steps.title: Write the abbreviated configuration
solution_steps.detail: After removing the Argon core, the remaining electrons are the $$4s^2$$ and $$3d^1$$ electrons, so the abbreviated configuration is $$[\text{Ar}]4s^2 3d^1$$.

solution_steps.title: Classify the element by its outermost filling subshell
solution_steps.detail: The last electron added enters the $$3d$$ subshell. Elements that are filling a $$d$$ subshell of the $$(n-1)$$ shell (here $$3d$$) are transition elements. The $$4s$$ subshell was filled first only because it is slightly lower in energy, so it does not change the classification.

solution_steps.title: State the conclusion
solution_steps.detail: The element is Scandium ($$Z = 21$$), abbreviated configuration $$[\text{Ar}]4s^2 3d^1$$, and it is a d-block transition element (not representative and not inner transition, because no $$f$$ subshell is being filled).

questions.answer: (a) Scandium ($$Sc$$), atomic number $$Z = 21$$. (b) $$[\text{Ar}]4s^2 3d^1$$. (c) A transition element, because its outermost occupied configuration is filling the $$3d$$ subshell of the $$(n-1)$$ shell.

similar_questions.question: A chemistry student writes the configuration of an atom as $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2 3d^{10} 4p^2$$. (a) Determine the atomic number of this element. (b) Write its abbreviated electron configuration using the correct noble gas core. (c) State whether it is an s-block, p-block or d-block element and name the block.
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$Z = 32$$ (Germanium). (b) $$[\text{Ar}]4s^2 3d^{10} 4p^2$$. (c) It is a p-block representative element, because the last electrons enter the $$4p$$ subshell.

solution_steps.title: Total the electrons
solution_steps.detail: $$2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 10 + 2 = 32$$, so the element has 32 protons and $$Z = 32$$.

solution_steps.title: Pick the preceding noble gas
solution_steps.detail: The noble gas directly above is Argon ($$Z = 18$$): $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6$$. Replacing that core gives $$[\text{Ar}]4s^2 3d^{10} 4p^2$$.

solution_steps.title: Determine the block
solution_steps.detail: The configuration ends in $$4p^2$$, so the outermost electrons are filling a $$p$$ subshell. Elements filling $$s$$ or $$p$$ subshells are representative elements, and this one belongs to the p-block.

solution_steps.title: State the conclusion
solution_steps.detail: The element is Germanium ($$Z = 32$$), abbreviated as $$[\text{Ar}]4s^2 3d^{10} 4p^2$$, a p-block representative element.

similar_questions.variant_note: Uses a longer configuration ending in a filled $$3d$$ plus $$4p^2$$, so the identification, the noble-gas core and the block classification (p-block instead of d-block) all differ from the main question.

similar_questions.question: A rare-earth ore sample contains an element with the abbreviated configuration $$[\text{Xe}]6s^2 4f^1$$. (a) Which subshell is being filled by the differentiating electron? (b) Classify the element as representative, transition or inner transition, giving your reason. (c) Explain why this element is placed in the two rows below the main body of the Periodic Table.
similar_questions.answer: (a) The $$4f$$ subshell is being filled. (b) It is an inner transition element, because the differentiating electron enters an $$f$$ subshell of the $$(n-2)$$ shell. (c) Inner transition elements fill $$f$$ subshells of the $$(n-2)$$ shell and are shown in the two separate rows (Lanthanide and Actinide series) below the main table to keep the table compact.

solution_steps.title: Locate the last subshell being filled
solution_steps.detail: Reading the configuration $$[\text{Xe}]6s^2 4f^1$$, the final electron is added to the $$4f$$ subshell, so this is the differentiating subshell.

solution_steps.title: Test this against the block definitions
solution_steps.detail: Representative elements fill $$s$$ or $$p$$ subshells, transition elements fill a $$d$$ subshell of the $$(n-1)$$ shell, and inner transition elements fill an $$f$$ subshell of the $$(n-2)$$ shell. Here $$n = 6$$ and the subshell is $$4f$$, i.e. $$(6-2)f$$, so the third definition applies.

solution_steps.title: Classify and explain the layout
solution_steps.detail: The element is an inner transition element of the Lanthanide series (filling $$4f$$). Because there are 14 such elements in each series, they are pulled out into two separate rows below the main body of the table so the main table does not become too wide.

solution_steps.title: State the conclusion
solution_steps.detail: The differentiating electron occupies $$4f$$; the element is an inner transition (f-block) element, shown in the Lanthanide row beneath the main table.

similar_questions.variant_note: Shifts the question from a d-block element to an f-block inner transition element and asks for the layout reason, testing the third block definition instead of the second.

questions.question: The element Phosphorus is an essential nutrient in Eritrean soils; a fertiliser bag in Asmara lists it as containing phosphorus ($$Z = 15$$). (a) Write the full electron configuration of phosphorus. (b) Identify the subshell occupied by the electron that differentiates phosphorus from the element before it. (c) How many unpaired electrons does a phosphorus atom have in its outermost shell, and which group of the Periodic Table does it therefore belong to?

solution_steps.title: Recall the Aufbau filling order
solution_steps.detail: Electrons fill subshells in order of increasing energy: $$1s \rightarrow 2s \rightarrow 2p \rightarrow 3s \rightarrow 3p \rightarrow 4s \rightarrow 3d \rightarrow 4p$$. Each subshell is filled to capacity before the next begins ($$s$$ holds 2, $$p$$ holds 6).

solution_steps.title: Distribute the 15 electrons
solution_steps.detail: $$1s^2$$ (2 electrons) + $$2s^2$$ (2) + $$2p^6$$ (6) + $$3s^2$$ (2) = 12 electrons; the remaining $$15 - 12 = 3$$ electrons go into the $$3p$$ subshell. The full configuration is $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^3$$.

solution_steps.title: Verify the electron count
solution_steps.detail: Adding the superscripts: $$2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 3 = 15$$, which matches $$Z = 15$$, so the configuration is correct.

solution_steps.title: Identify the differentiating subshell
solution_steps.detail: The element preceding phosphorus is Silicon ($$Z = 14$$, configuration $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^2$$). The extra electron in phosphorus enters the $$3p$$ subshell, so $$3p$$ is the differentiating subshell.

solution_steps.title: Count the unpaired electrons
solution_steps.detail: The three $$3p$$ electrons enter the three separate $$3p$$ orbitals singly before any pairing occurs, so none of them is paired: phosphorus has 3 unpaired electrons in its outermost shell. This is the same half-filled $$p$$-subshell situation the chapter describes for nitrogen ($$2p^3$$).

solution_steps.title: Determine the group and conclude
solution_steps.detail: The outermost shell is $$n = 3$$ with the configuration $$3s^2 3p^3$$, giving 5 valence electrons, so phosphorus lies in Group VA (Group 15), the nitrogen family.

questions.answer: (a) $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^3$$ (or $$[\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^3$$). (b) The $$3p$$ subshell. (c) 3 unpaired electrons, so phosphorus belongs to Group VA (Group 15) with 5 valence electrons.

similar_questions.question: Sulfur ($$Z = 16$$) is recovered from natural gas deposits and used to make sulfuric acid. (a) Write the full electron configuration of a sulfur atom. (b) State how many electrons are in its outermost principal shell. (c) State how many of those outer electrons are unpaired, and name the group of the Periodic Table to which sulfur belongs.
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^4$$. (b) 6 electrons in the $$n = 3$$ shell. (c) 2 unpaired electrons; sulfur belongs to Group VIA (Group 16).

solution_steps.title: Fill the subshells in Aufbau order
solution_steps.detail: Following $$1s \rightarrow 2s \rightarrow 2p \rightarrow 3s \rightarrow 3p$$: $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^4$$. Check: $$2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 4 = 16$$ electrons, matching $$Z = 16$$.

solution_steps.title: Count the outermost-shell electrons
solution_steps.detail: The outermost shell is $$n = 3$$, containing $$3s^2 3p^4$$, so there are $$2 + 4 = 6$$ electrons in that shell.

solution_steps.title: Account for the unpaired $$3p$$ electrons
solution_steps.detail: The four $$3p$$ electrons fill the three $$3p$$ orbitals singly first (3 unpaired), then the fourth pairs up in one orbital. So the number unpaired is $$3 - 1 = 2$$, and the two $$3s$$ electrons are already paired.

solution_steps.title: Name the group
solution_steps.detail: With 6 valence electrons ($$3s^2 3p^4$$), sulfur is the second member of Group VIA (Group 16), below oxygen.

similar_questions.variant_note: Replaces phosphorus ($$3p^3$$, 3 unpaired, Group VA) with sulfur ($$3p^4$$, 2 unpaired, Group VIA), so both the configuration and the unpaired-electron count change.

similar_questions.question: Carbon ($$Z = 6$$) forms the backbone of all organic molecules, including the carbohydrates in Eritrean teff and sorghum. (a) Write the full electron configuration of carbon. (b) How many unpaired electrons does a carbon atom have in its outermost shell? (c) Explain, using the idea of unpaired valence electrons, why carbon forms the chloride $$CCl_4$$ and not $$CCl_2$$.
similar_questions.answer: (a) $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^2$$. (b) 2 unpaired electrons (in the $$2p$$ subshell). (c) Carbon has 4 valence electrons available for bonding ($$2s^2 2p^2$$), so four chlorine atoms each share one electron pair with carbon, giving $$CCl_4$$; $$CCl_2$$ would leave two of carbon's valence electrons unbonded.

solution_steps.title: Write the configuration
solution_steps.detail: Filling in energy order for 6 electrons: $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^2$$. Check: $$2 + 2 + 2 = 6$$, matching $$Z = 6$$.

solution_steps.title: Count unpaired electrons
solution_steps.detail: The two $$2p$$ electrons occupy two different $$2p$$ orbitals singly, so carbon has 2 unpaired $$p$$ electrons; the $$2s$$ pair is paired.

solution_steps.title: Relate valence electrons to bonding capacity
solution_steps.detail: Carbon's outer shell is $$2s^2 2p^2$$, giving 4 valence electrons (the two $$2s$$ electrons are promoted and shared in bonding in the chapter's valency picture). Each valence electron can take part in one shared pair, so carbon can form 4 bonds.

solution_steps.title: Apply this to the chlorides
solution_steps.detail: With 4 bonding electrons, carbon bonds to 4 chlorine atoms and forms $$CCl_4$$. The formula $$CCl_2$$ would use only 2 of the 4 available valence electrons and would leave 2 electrons unshared, so it is not the normal chloride.

similar_questions.variant_note: Uses carbon and links the electron configuration to compound formulas ($$CCl_4$$) instead of phosphorus and group position, keeping the same Aufbau filling and unpaired-electron reasoning.

questions.question: Sodium ($$Na$$, $$Z = 11$$) and Chlorine ($$Cl$$, $$Z = 17$$) both lie in period 3 of the Periodic Table, yet they behave very differently: sodium is a soft reactive metal while chlorine is a reactive nonmetal. Using the ideas of nuclear charge and shielding, (a) compare the atomic radii of the two atoms, (b) compare their first ionization energies, and (c) explain why sodium tends to lose an electron while chlorine tends to gain one.

solution_steps.title: Establish that both elements are in the same period
solution_steps.detail: Both Na ($$Z = 11$$) and Cl ($$Z = 17$$) fill electrons up to the third shell, so both have the same number of occupied shells ($$n = 1, 2, 3$$) and their outer electrons experience a similar amount of shielding by the inner $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$$ core.

solution_steps.title: Compare nuclear charge across the period
solution_steps.detail: The nuclear charge rises from $$+11$$ in sodium to $$+17$$ in chlorine while the shielding from the inner core stays the same, so the effective nuclear charge pulling on the outer electrons is much greater in chlorine.

solution_steps.title: Compare the atomic radii
solution_steps.detail: Across a period the number of shells is constant but the atomic number increases, so the extra nuclear charge pulls the outer electrons closer to the nucleus. The atomic radius therefore decreases from left to right, meaning Na is larger than Cl: $$r(\text{Na}) > r(\text{Cl})$$.

solution_steps.title: Compare the first ionization energies
solution_steps.detail: Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove the outermost electron from a neutral gaseous atom. Because the chlorine atom is smaller and its nucleus holds the outer electrons more tightly, more energy is required to remove an electron from chlorine than from sodium. So $$IE(\text{Cl}) > IE(\text{Na})$$, and the trend across a period is increasing ionization energy.

solution_steps.title: Explain the tendency to lose or gain electrons
solution_steps.detail: Sodium's outer electron is in a single $$3s^1$$ orbital, is far from the nucleus and is well shielded, so it is easy to remove; sodium therefore loses one electron to form $$Na^+$$ and behaves as a metal. Chlorine has seven valence electrons ($$3s^2 3p^5$$) and a high nuclear charge, so it strongly attracts an extra electron to complete its outer shell, forming $$Cl^-$$ and behaving as a nonmetal.

solution_steps.title: State the overall conclusion
solution_steps.detail: Across period 3 from sodium to chlorine, atomic radius decreases while ionization energy and electronegativity increase; this explains why the metallic character falls and the nonmetallic character rises, so Na loses electrons and Cl gains them.

questions.answer: (a) The atomic radius of Na is larger than that of Cl ($$r(\text{Na}) > r(\text{Cl})$$), because nuclear charge increases across the period while the number of shells and the shielding stay the same. (b) The first ionization energy of Cl is greater than that of Na ($$IE(\text{Cl}) > IE(\text{Na})$$), because chlorine's smaller size and higher nuclear charge hold the outer electrons more tightly. (c) Sodium loses its loosely held $$3s^1$$ electron to form $$Na^+$$ (metallic character), whereas chlorine, with 7 valence electrons and a high nuclear charge, attracts an extra electron to form $$Cl^-$$ (nonmetallic character).

similar_questions.question: Magnesium ($$Mg$$, $$Z = 12$$) and Sulfur ($$S$$, $$Z = 16$$) are both period 3 elements. A student measured the atomic radii and first ionization energies of the two atoms and was surprised that sulfur's radius is smaller but its ionization energy is larger. Explain these two trends using nuclear charge and shielding, and state the general periodic trends they illustrate.
similar_questions.answer: Sulfur has a smaller atomic radius and a larger first ionization energy than magnesium. Across a period the number of shells and the inner shielding stay the same while the nuclear charge increases from $$+12$$ (Mg) to $$+16$$ (S), so the outer electrons are pulled in more tightly (smaller radius) and need more energy to remove (higher ionization energy). The trends are: atomic radius decreases across a period, and ionization energy increases across a period.

solution_steps.title: Confirm the shared period
solution_steps.detail: Mg ($$Z = 12$$) and S ($$Z = 16$$) both have their outer electrons in the third shell, so they have the same number of occupied shells and similar shielding by the inner $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$$ core.

solution_steps.title: Explain the radius trend
solution_steps.detail: Moving from Mg to S, the nuclear charge increases by 4 units while the shielding is essentially unchanged. The stronger net pull draws the outer electrons closer, so the radius decreases: $$r(\text{Mg}) > r(\text{S})$$.

solution_steps.title: Explain the ionization-energy trend
solution_steps.detail: Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove the outermost electron from a neutral gaseous atom. Because sulfur's outer electrons are closer to the nucleus and held more tightly, more energy is needed to remove one, so $$IE(\text{S}) > IE(\text{Mg})$$.

solution_steps.title: State the general trends
solution_steps.detail: The two observations illustrate the core periodic trends across a period: atomic radius decreases, while ionization energy (and electronegativity) increases from left to right.

similar_questions.variant_note: Changes the pair from Na/Cl to Mg/S and asks for an explanation of observed measurements, but uses the same nuclear-charge and shielding reasoning.

similar_questions.question: Potassium ($$K$$, $$Z = 19$$) lies directly below Sodium ($$Na$$, $$Z = 11$$) in Group IA. State and explain how the atomic radius and the first ionization energy change when descending the group from sodium to potassium, and explain why potassium is the more reactive metal.
similar_questions.answer: Descending Group IA from Na to K, the atomic radius increases and the first ionization energy decreases. Each step down adds a new energy shell, so the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and shielded by more core electrons; it is therefore easier to remove, which makes potassium more reactive than sodium.

solution_steps.title: Compare the shell structures
solution_steps.detail: Sodium has its outer electron in the third shell ($$[\text{Ne}]3s^1$$), while potassium adds a fourth shell ($$[\text{Ar}]4s^1$$). Potassium therefore has one more occupied shell.

solution_steps.title: Apply the down-a-group radius trend
solution_steps.detail: Although the nuclear charge increases, the addition of a new shell increases the physical distance of the outer electron from the nucleus and increases shielding by the core electrons, and this overcomes the extra nuclear pull. The atomic radius therefore increases down the group: $$r(\text{K}) > r(\text{Na})$$.

solution_steps.title: Apply the down-a-group ionization-energy trend
solution_steps.detail: Because the outer $$4s^1$$ electron of potassium is farther from the nucleus and more heavily shielded than the $$3s^1$$ electron of sodium, less energy is required to remove it. The first ionization energy therefore decreases down the group: $$IE(\text{Na}) > IE(\text{K})$$.

solution_steps.title: Link this to reactivity
solution_steps.detail: Metallic character increases down a group because the valence electron is lost more easily. Potassium gives up its outer electron more readily than sodium, so it is the more reactive metal, and both form singly positive ions ($$Na^+$$, $$K^+$$).

similar_questions.variant_note: Switches the comparison from across a period (Na vs Cl) to down a group (Na vs K), so the radius increases and the ionization energy decreases instead of the reverse.
